entities.summary:
David Kimhi (1160–1235), known by the Hebrew acronym RaDaK (רַדָּ״ק), was a preeminent Provençal rabbi, biblical commentator, grammarian, and philosopher whose work profoundly shaped both Jewish and Christian biblical scholarship across the late Medieval and early Modern periods. Born into a distinguished family of scholars in Narbonne, he inherited and advanced the rationalist tradition of his father, Joseph Kimhi, and his elder brother, Moses Kimhi, becoming a pivotal figure in the golden age of Jewish learning in Provence and a bridge between Sephardic linguistic rigor and Ashkenazic exegetical depth.

Kimhi's most significant literary contributions include the "Sefer Mikhlol" (Book of Completeness), a comprehensive treatise on Hebrew grammar and a dictionary of biblical Hebrew roots, which systematized the language for generations of students. His biblical commentaries, covering most of the Hebrew Bible, are renowned for their clear, concise Pshat (literal) interpretations, meticulous grammatical analysis, and engagement with philosophical concepts, often defending Jewish tradition against Karaite and Christian polemics. He served as a communal leader and diplomat, notably participating in the Maimonidean controversy, advocating for the study of philosophy and rational inquiry within Jewish thought.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: David Kimhi's systematization of Hebrew grammar and his literal biblical commentaries became indispensable for both Jewish and Christian scholars for centuries, profoundly shaping biblical exegesis during the Renaissance and Reformation. His works facilitated the transmission of Sephardic linguistic rigor across Europe, influencing figures like Johannes Reuchlin and Martin Luther.
